evidence.source_sentence: Aromatic and aliphatic polyamidines of the common structure $- ( \mathbf { R } _ { 1 } - \mathbf { N } = \mathbf { C } ( \mathbf { R } _ { 2 } ) - \mathbf { N } \mathbf { H } ) _ { n } -$were investigated by electrokinetic measurements in dependence on the pH value.
It could be evidenced, that all polyamidine surfaces show Brønsted basic behaviour.

It was found that in the case of aromatic polyamidines $( \mathbf { R } _ { 1 } = \mathrm { a r y l } )$the charge density is dependent on specific interactions of the amidine groups in the solid phase.
Especially, in polyformamidines mutual shielding of the amidine groups by hydrogen bonds resulted in reduced charge densities on the surface.
Keywords: Polyamidines; Surface properties; Electrokinetic investigation; Zeta potential; Acid–base properties
The synthesis of the aromatic polyamidines 1a– 1e was described earlier [7].

The aliphatic polyamidines 1f and 1g were synthesized as follows: A mixture of 47.5 mmol of 1,10-decanediamine, 50 mmol of triethylorthobenzoate or triethylorthoacetate, respectively, and 40 mmol of acetic acid was heated under nitrogen from 80 to $1 2 0 \mathrm { { } ^ { \circ } C }$with stirring and continuous removing of the resulting alcohol by distillation.
A similar procedure was used for 1h.
The structure of the polymers 1a–1g was confirmed by NMR and titration of the amidine groups.
Polyamidine 1h was insoluble and infusible.
A total of 100 mg of polyamidine were dissolved in 40 ml ethanol (1f–1g) or DMSO (1a–1e) and titrated with 1 N aqueous HCl standard solution.
Compared to the procedure used for the preparation of the aromatic polyamidines 1a–1e [7] the reaction conditions for the preparation of 1f–1h were changed.
It has to be mentioned that in case of 1f and 1g the acetic acid was strongly bonded to the polymers and could only be removed under drastic conditions.
Electrokinetic measurements of the polyamidines in dependence on the pH-value were carried out in electrolytic solutions.

With a help of a computer program [17,18] $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$values of the polyamidine surfaces among other parameters were calculated.
Because of their lower relevance in comparing surface properties of polyamidines the other parameter are not given here.

For comparison purposes $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$values of the polyamidines in solution were determined by titration with 0.1 N aqueous HCl in DMSO (1a–1e) and ethanol (1f and 1g), respectively.
As an example the titration curve of the polyamidine 1f is shown in Fig.
The results clearly show that the surface properties of the polyamidines correlate with their basic behaviour in solution.
The aromatic polyamidines 1a–1e possess isoelectric points at relatively low pH values in the range 7.0–8.0 and $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$values on the surface between 7.2 and 8.1.
The highest values were found for the polyacylamidines 1b–1d since the alkyl residues at the amidine group rather act as electron donor than the proton in 1a or the phenyl group in 1e.
Distinctly more pronounced basicity were shown by polyamidines substituted with aliphatic groups on both nitrogens.
The isoelectric point of 1h was found at pH 11.2 and that one of 1g was beyond the measuring range of our equipment.
Polyamidine 1f could not be investigated by electrokinetic measurements since it was liquid at room temperature, but its $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$in solution reveals medium basicity.

It is remarkable that the magnitude of the zeta potential $( \zeta _ { \mathrm { p l a t e a u } } { \cdot } \mathrm { v a l u e } )$of polyformamidine 1a is distinctly decreased compared to the other aromatic polyamidines 1b–1e (see Fig.
The calculated $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { d i f f } }$values of the polyamidines 1a–1h are shown in Table 2.
The distinctly lower $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { d i f f } }$and $\zeta _ { \mathrm { p l a t e a u } }$-values of the polyformamidine 1a can be explained by its solid phase structure.
In contrast with this, E-anti configuration is predominant in polyamidines 1b–1e.

Although a direct comparison with the aliphatic polyamidines is problematic due to the completely different structure it seems that the relatively low $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { d i f f } }$value of 1h is also caused by interactions in the bulk.

It is remarkable that the magnitude of the zeta potential $( \zeta _ { \mathrm { p l a t e a u } } { \cdot } \mathrm { v a l u e } )$of polyformamidine 1a is distinctly decreased compared to the other aromatic polyamidines 1b–1e (see Fig. 1).
Zeta potential measurements were carried out on pulverized samples suspended in electrolytic solutions (0.01 wt.%) using a Zeta Sizer 3 (Malvern Instruments, Malvern, Worcestershire, UK).

The aliphatic polyamidines 1f and 1g were synthesized as follows: A mixture of 47.5 mmol of 1,10-decanediamine, 50 mmol of triethylorthobenzoate or triethylorthoacetate, respectively, and 40 mmol of acetic acid was heated under nitrogen from 80 to $1 2 0 \mathrm { { } ^ { \circ } C }$with stirring and continuous removing of the resulting alcohol by distillation. The temperature was kept for 105 min at $1 2 0 \mathrm { { } ^ { \circ } C }$. Then the pressure was reduced to 5 mbar and the temperature was raised stepwise to $1 8 0 \mathrm { { } ^ { \circ } C }$within 45 min. After another 135 min the reaction was completed.
A similar procedure was used for 1h. Since solidification occurred during the synthesis the temperature was finally raised to $2 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$

Zeta potential measurements were carried out on pulverized samples suspended in electrolytic solutions (0.01 wt.%) using a Zeta Sizer 3 (Malvern Instruments, Malvern, Worcestershire, UK). The velocity of the particles in an electric field of 100 V was measured by Laser Doppler Anemometry using a He/Ne laser beam. The simple Smoluchowski equation which allows to calculate zeta potential values from the electrophoretic mobilities - was used:

The amidine group content of the polymers was determined by potentiometric titration using a Mettler DL 70 titrator (electrode Mettler DG 113-SC). A total of 100 mg of polyamidine were dissolved in 40 ml ethanol (1f–1g) or DMSO (1a–1e) and titrated with 1 N aqueous HCl standard solution.
